GK-09.c01: A **hazard** is any road condition or road user that could become a danger; an **emergency** is danger happening now.
Seeing hazards early gives you time to check mirrors, signal, slow down or change lanes calmly instead of braking hard or swerving.
Hazards often come with **clues**, and you get better at reading them with experience.
GK-09.c02: Approaching a stopped emergency vehicle or work zone → **slow down and move to a lane not next to it**, if safe; otherwise slow down and pass carefully.
[CA] Breaking the move-over law is an **infraction** punished by a fine (**CVC §21809**).
In work zones drive slowly and warn drivers behind with **4-way flashers or brake lights**; keep away from pavement **drop-offs**.
Avoid foreign objects **without sudden moves**, and on ramps be slow enough **before** the curve, since posted ramp speeds may be too fast for trucks.
GK-09.c03: Watch for people who **can't see or hear you**: blocked windows, rental trucks, delivery trucks, parked cars, bus passengers, pedestrians with headphones.
If you see part of a vehicle but **not the driver**, assume the driver can't see you and be ready to stop.
Confused drivers, slow vehicles and impaired drivers act unpredictably; [CA] a vehicle with the **SMV emblem** (red triangle, orange center) is not designed to exceed **25 mph**.
Impaired-driver clues include weaving, stopping at a green light, and a **window open in cold weather**; watch especially late at night.
A **conflict** means you must change speed, direction, or both to avoid a hit; other drivers' conflicts can become yours.
GK-09.c04: Hazards can turn into emergencies, so when you see one, **picture the emergency** it could cause and decide what you would do.
Being ready to act on that plan is **defensive driving**.
GK-09.c05: **Driver distraction** is anything that pulls your attention off driving, risking injury, death or property damage.
Distractions can be **inside** the vehicle (passengers, radio, eating, phone, CB, texting, telematics, daydreaming) or **outside** (crash scenes, sunlight, objects, billboards).
GK-09.c06: In the LTCCS, **8%** of large-truck crashes involved a distraction outside the vehicle and **2%** a distraction inside.
Distracted-driving crashes kill about **5,500** and injure about **448,000** people a year in the U.S. (NHTSA).
A phone conversation, **even hands-free**, takes **39%** of the brain energy you normally use for driving.
GK-09.c07: Distraction causes **slowed perception**, so you notice important events late or never.
It causes **delayed decision making**, so you are slow to choose the right action.
It causes **improper action**, such as wrong steering, gas or brake input.
GK-09.c08: **Physical** distraction takes your hands from the wheel or eyes from the road, like reaching for an object.
**Mental** distraction takes your mind off the road, like talking with a passenger.
Distractions that are **both**, like phone calls and texting, carry the **greatest** crash risk.
GK-09.c09: CMV drivers may not use **hand-held** phones while driving: holding the phone for a call, dialing more than one button, or leaving your seat-belted position to reach it.
2nd conviction in 3 years → **60-day** disqualification; 3rd or more in 3 years → **120 days**; hand-held use is allowed only to contact law enforcement or emergency services.
Dialing makes a safety-critical event **6 times** more likely and takes eyes off the road **3.8 seconds**, about 306 feet at 55 mph.
Hands-free devices are **no less distracting** than hand-held ones; [CA] devices are legal while driving only in hands-free mode.
If you must use a device, keep it short, **hang up** in difficult traffic, and never type or read messages.
GK-09.c10: CMV drivers may not **text** while driving in interstate commerce, including reading or entering text, email, or web pages.
Penalties: **60 days** disqualification (2nd in 3 years), 120 days (3rd+ in 3 years), and civil penalties **up to $2,750** per violation.
Texting makes a safety-critical event **23.2 times** more likely, with eyes off the road **4.6 seconds**, about 371 feet at 55 mph.
The only exception is contacting **law enforcement or emergency services**.
GK-09.c11: Remove **all** in-vehicle distractions before driving, because reacting just **half a second** slower doubles crashes.
Turn off devices; if you must use a phone, keep it **within reach while buckled in** and use hands-free features.
Before driving, adjust controls and mirrors, preset radio, secure loose objects and cargo, and **set the GPS**; avoid eating, smoking and emotional conversations.
GK-09.c12: Signs of a distracted driver include **drifting** over or within lane lines, changing speeds, and being busy with maps, food, phones or passengers.
Give them **plenty of room**, keep a safe following distance, and pass very carefully, since they may drift in front of you.
GK-09.c13: **Aggressive driving** is driving in a selfish, bold or pushy way, ignoring others' rights and safety, like frequent unsignaled lane changes.
**Road rage** is driving with intent to harm others, or physically attacking a driver or their vehicle.
Heavy, slow traffic and tight schedules make drivers angry and quick to take others' mistakes personally.
GK-09.c14: Your **mood before you start** strongly affects how stress hits you, so lower stress before and during the drive.
Be realistic about travel time; if you'll be late, **accept it**, and give others the benefit of the doubt.
Slow down, stay out of the left lane when slower than traffic, **avoid gestures**, and let others in ("Be my guest").
GK-09.c15: First and most important → **get out of their way**; put your pride aside and don't speed up or hold your lane.
Report the vehicle's **license number**, description, location and direction; if they crash later, stop a safe distance away and wait for police.
